Chapter Eight: Mentorship, Legacy, and the Next Generation.
You know, after years of pushing through challenges and fighting those big battles, there’s a quiet shift that happens. Suddenly, it’s not just about the struggle—it’s about looking ahead, and nurturing the folks who’ll carry things forward.
For anyone who’s spent decades in the thick of it, there’s this deep urge to share what you’ve learned. The work’s not finished, not by a long shot, but the hope is that others will pick up the torch and run with it.
In the studio, things started to change. Young interns would show up, full of energy and ideas, ready to learn everything they could. They weren’t afraid to ask tough questions or shake things up. Watching them move through the world of radio and activism felt almost like looking in a mirror—remembering those first steps, that mix of excitement and nerves.
Mentorship wasn’t about handing down a list of rules. Instead, it became this daily rhythm of listening, encouraging, and just sharing stories. Sometimes, the advice was super practical—like how to dig deep on research, handle those tough interviews, or stay cool when the pressure’s on. Other times, it was all about resilience. How do you bounce back after a setback? How do you keep moving when things feel impossible?
I’ll never forget one afternoon when a young producer pulled me aside. She was worried about making mistakes on air—scared she’d mess up in front of everyone. All I could say was, “Everyone stumbles. What matters is getting back up.” Simple words, sure. But when you say them with the weight of experience, they stick. Over time, she found her voice—and let me tell you, her confidence soared.
The mentorship didn’t stop at the studio doors. Out in the community, leaders ran workshops for high school students, teaching the basics of organizing, public speaking, and the real history behind the movement. Elders would share stories about both victories and defeats, making sure the younger generation knew they weren’t starting from scratch—they were part of something much bigger.
That sense of legacy? It’s powerful. Every new activist, every curious journalist, becomes a link in a chain that stretches into the future. The hope is simple: that they’ll learn from what came before, take what works, and chart their own path forward. The goal isn’t to be remembered as some kind of hero, but to stay part of a community that never stops fighting for justice.
Years pass, and the faces in the studio always change. But the mission? That stays the same. Mentorship is never really finished. And every fresh voice you hear is proof that the struggle—and the hope—will always keep going.
